Loaded deposit_not_returned. Its instructions:

# Deposit not returned

Rests on 83.49 (the deposit) and 83.505 (notices by e-mail). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes").

## First, whether this applies

- 83.49 does not cover every deposit: "This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs" (83.49(4)). It then says: "With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes." (83.49(4)).
  - The landlord is a housing authority or public housing agency: (3), (5), and (6) still apply, so this skill still applies.
  - A private landlord in a government housing program: not settled. The text names programs by section number and does not say which tenant subsidies they cover. Give both readings and choose neither. One: the rent or deposit counts as regulated, so 83.49 does not apply (what does is outside this tool). The other: only a program that sets or limits the amount of the rent or of the deposit does that, so 83.49 applies. Name both, rent and deposit, as 83.49(4) does.
- College housing may be outside part II. It does not apply to "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (83.42(1)). Settle this once for the matter, in this order, and never ask it twice:
  - The facts already hold school_housing, pending or confirmed: use it, and do not ask again.
  - Otherwise read the lease: who the landlord is, and whether living there is tied to a school, to being enrolled, or to services a school provides. The lease is clear only if nothing in it points to a school and nothing leaves doubt. Treat it as not clear if it has anything like: a clause on enrollment or attendance (the landlord may ask about it, or end the lease if the tenant is not enrolled, suspended, or expelled); a title or terms for students, or housing only for students; a school named as owner, manager, or partner; rooms assigned by a school; services a school provides (meals, advising, resident programs); a term set by the school year or semesters; or anything else that leaves doubt. If the lease is clear, say what it shows in one line, cite the lease, and note it with note_fact as school_housing (tenant_words: "from the lease").
  - If the lease does not make it clear, ask the tenant one plain question: is the housing run by or for their school, or can they live there only while enrolled? Note the answer with note_fact as school_housing.
  - Read 83.42 before telling the tenant whether the exclusion applies.
- Money the lease calls nonrefundable may fall under 83.491. Read it before treating that money as outside 83.49.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- school_housing: whether living there comes with the tenant's schooling (see "First, whether this applies").
- public_housing: whether a housing authority is the landlord, or a government housing program (public housing, Section 8, a subsidized building) pays part of the rent or sets it. Ask only if the lease or the tenant points to one.
- lease_end_date: the date the rental agreement ended (for a renewal, the renewal's end: "a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement" (83.49(6))). move_out_date: the date they moved out and returned the keys.
- Whether they moved out before the lease's end, or had a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy.
- If so: what written notice they gave before leaving, how it reached the landlord, and whether it gave an address.
- What the landlord sent about keeping any of the deposit: what it said, how it came, the date on it (claim_notice_date), and the date the tenant received it (claim_received_date).
- Whether they and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail.
- forwarding_address: whether they gave the landlord a new mailing address, which one, and when (ask only if a notice came by mail). The statute's disclosure to tenants says "YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT" (83.49(2)(d)).

## Option 1: the whole deposit, because no notice of a claim came in time

All three conditions must be met. Settle each one from the facts: met, not met, the tenant can tell us, or not settled.

1. **No proper notice of a claim reached the tenant.** The rule: "If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim." (83.49(3)(a)). E-mail counts only "if the parties have signed an addendum to the rental agreement that the parties specifically agree to the electronic delivery of notices" (83.505(1)).
   - Nothing in writing about keeping any of it arrived: met.
   - A notice came by certified mail, to the new address the tenant gave (the old one, if they gave none), or by e-mail under a signed addendum: not met. Say so in one sentence: this is the kind of notice the statute requires, so on this ground the landlord has not lost its claim. Then go to option 2.
   - A notice came some other way (regular mail, a text, a portal message, by hand), or by certified mail to the old address after the tenant gave a new one (the text does not define the last known mailing address): not settled. Give both readings and choose neither. One: it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited (the forfeiture sentence below). The other: a notice the tenant actually received in time is enough, since 83.505 "does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). Under that reading, go on to option 2 as well and give both of its dates, and say what each reading means for the tenant's money.
   - A notice came the right way but gives no reason for the claim: met. It is not the required notice, since the rule asks for "the reason for imposing the claim" (83.49(3)(a)).
   - A notice came the right way and gives the reason but leaves out the amount, the warning to object within 15 days, or where to send an objection. Those are parts of "a statement in substantially the following form" (83.49(3)(a)), not of the rule's own words: not settled whether it is still the required notice. Give both readings and choose neither. One: without that part it is not the required notice, so the claim is forfeited. The other: the form need only be followed substantially, so it is still enough. Under that reading, go on to option 2 and give both of its dates.
2. **The 30 days have passed.** Call count_days(lease_end_date, 30). If it has not passed, a notice may still come in time, so this option is not open yet.
   - If the tenant moved out before the lease's end date, which date ends the rental agreement is not settled. Call both count_days(lease_end_date, 30) and count_days(move_out_date, 30), and give both readings. The lease end date: 83.49(3)(a) begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)), naming vacating and termination as two things. The move-out date: the required disclosure tells tenants the notice comes "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)).
3. **The landlord was not relieved of the notice.** A tenant who left early, or had a periodic tenancy, must give notice first. Who: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year," (83.49(5)). How: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." (83.49(5)).
   - The tenant stayed to the lease's end and had no periodic tenancy: met.
   - They gave that notice, with an address, on or before the date count_days(move_out_date, -7) gives: met.
   - The lease sets a different rule on notice before leaving, and they followed it: met. Read the lease's clause.
   - Otherwise not met: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)). Say both halves: the landlord's silence forfeits nothing, and the tenant keeps the right to the deposit.

If all three are met: "If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant." (83.49(3)(a)). Say both halves: the whole deposit comes back, and the landlord may still sue for damages after.

## Option 2: the balance after a notice of a claim

When a notice of a claim came (or under the reading that one that came another way counts): "Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages." (83.49(3)(b)).

- The tenant's last day to object in writing: count_days(claim_received_date, 15).
- The landlord's last day to send the balance: count_days(claim_notice_date, 30).
- If the tenant objected within the 15 days: the right to deduct and the duty to remit the balance are in a sentence that begins "Unless the tenant objects" (83.49(3)(b)). The text sets no step after an objection, only a court action (below). Do not say the landlord may deduct or that the balance is overdue; say what follows is not settled.
- Not objecting is not the end: "The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action." (83.49(3)(b)).

## The 15-day return

When the landlord intends no claim: "if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). The date: count_days(lease_end_date, 15). Passing it forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a notice of a claim are still running.

## Court costs and fees

Only if someone sues, and only for the winner: "If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney." (83.49(3)(c)). The same paragraph adds: "The court shall advance the cause on the calendar." (83.49(3)(c)). Say it plainly: the court hears such a case sooner.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Writing any date that count_days did not give you, or comparing dates yourself.
- Saying the landlord forfeits before count_days shows the 30 days passed, or when a proper notice came.
- Stopping at the forfeiture without saying the landlord may still sue for damages.
- Leaving out 83.49(5) when the tenant left early or had a periodic tenancy.
- Promising court costs or fees without the condition in 83.49(3)(c).
- Leaning toward one reading of a point that is not settled, as in "probably yes".
- Telling a tenant of a housing authority that 83.49 does not apply.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded repair_not_made. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when something in the unit needs repair and the landlord has not fixed it: the roof, a window or a door, a floor, steps, or a porch, an outside wall or the foundation, pipes, drains, toilets, or faucets, heat, running water, hot water, the air conditioning, an appliance, pests, locks or keys, electrical work, mold, or a common area such as a hallway.

It covers two things the tenant may do about it: end the lease, or not pay rent because of the problem and raise it as a defense if the landlord sues for possession. It also covers the written notice each one starts from. It does not decide whether a local building, housing, or health code covers the problem; the tool does not hold those codes.

If the landlord has also sent a written demand for unpaid rent, or has filed an eviction case, load notice_received_nonpayment too.

The statute leaves some housing out of this part: "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)) This matters when the tenant lives in college housing. The tool records the facts and does not decide whether this applies to the tenant's housing. Say that it could matter and that the tool does not decide it.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; you apply the term to their answer.

### From the lease (search_lease)

- The maintenance and repairs clause: does it say the landlord repairs this kind of problem, and does an exception leave this problem out (such as damage caused by a roommate or a guest)? Try a second wording if the first finds nothing.
- The notices clause: where and how the tenant's written notice must be sent to the landlord, and whether it mentions notices by e-mail.
- Anything it says about repairs the tenant pays for.

### From the tenant

- What the problem is, in their own words, and which part of the unit it is with. Offer the plain choices: the roof; a window or a door; a floor, steps, or a porch; an outside wall or the foundation; another part of the building's structure; pipes, drains, toilets, or faucets; heat; running water; hot water; the air conditioning; an appliance; pests; locks or keys; electrical; mold; a common area; something else.
- When it started, or when they first noticed it.
- Whether they rent a single-family house or a duplex, rather than a unit in an apartment building or a dorm.
- Who or what caused it, as far as they know: nothing anyone did (age, wear, weather), the landlord or its workers, they themselves, a family member who lives with them, a guest or someone else they let in, a roommate, someone they did not let in (a neighbor, a stranger), or they do not know.
- Whether they have sent the landlord or the office anything in writing about it (a letter, an e-mail, a resident portal request, a text). If so: how it reached the landlord (handed over, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal, a text, something else); the date it reached the landlord (the day it was handed over or sent, or the delivery date on a mail receipt); whether it says anything about ending the lease or moving out; whether it says anything about not paying rent; and the sentences that say what they asked for and what they will do if the problem is not fixed, word for word. If they sent more than one, ask about the one that says the most about what they will do.
- Whether they have paid rent since they knew about the problem.
- What the landlord has said or done about it so far.
- Whether the landlord has filed an eviction case against them.

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes the two 7-day deadlines (see Deadlines) only from facts the tenant has confirmed: the date the tenant's written message was delivered to the landlord, whether that message says they intend to end the lease because of the problem, and whether it says they intend not to pay rent because of it. When the tenant tells you one of these, propose it for their record, so they can confirm it.

### Evidence worth keeping

- Photos or video of the condition, with dates.
- The written notice, with proof of how and when it was delivered.
- Every reply from the landlord, with dates.
- Any code enforcement complaint or inspection report.
- Rent receipts for the months since the problem started.

## What the tenant can do

Before any step, say whether the tenant can do it, what that turns on, and what is left to do. Each condition below is settled in one of four ways. The lease can settle it: read that clause with search_lease and say what it says. The tenant can tell you. It is not settled: give the open question from the section below. Or it is outside the tool: say what to check and where.

### End the lease because the landlord has not made the repair

The statute's answer to a landlord who does not act: "the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) The full sentence is under Deadlines. All four conditions need to be met.

1. The landlord had a duty to fix this problem, under 83.51(1) or a material provision of the lease. The statute reaches a failure to comply with 83.51(1) "or material provisions of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). Any one of these ways meets it:
   - The problem is with the structure or the plumbing. 83.51(1)(b) says: "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(b)). The tenant's pick tells you: the roof, a window or door, a floor, steps, or porch, an outside wall or the foundation, another structural part, or pipes, drains, toilets, or faucets. Any other pick is not plainly one of these parts.
   - The problem is running water or hot water. It may be the plumbing 83.51(1)(b) names, or an item only 83.51(2)(a) names: "Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water." (Fla. Stat. 83.51(2)(a)) This is not settled; give the open question on subsection (1) or (2).
   - The tenant picked 'something else'. Ask what the problem is with, beside the structural parts and the plumbing 83.51(1)(b) names.
   - The lease says the landlord repairs this problem (lease). Read the maintenance and repairs clause, say what it says, and say whether an exception leaves this problem out.
   - A building, housing, or health code where the unit is requires the landlord to fix it: "Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(a)). This is outside the tool. The city or county code enforcement office can say whether a code covers the problem, and can inspect the unit. Send the tenant there.
2. The landlord's duty was not changed in writing. The statute names a change in writing only for one kind of home: "The landlord’s obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex." (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)) This is met when the tenant's unit is not a single-family home or duplex (tenant). If it is one, read the lease's maintenance and repairs clause (lease), and ask whether they signed anything else that changes who repairs. The tool does not decide the effect of such a writing.
3. The tenant's side did not cause the problem: "The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant’s family, or other person on the premises with the tenant’s consent." (Fla. Stat. 83.51(4)) Met when the cause is nothing anyone did, the landlord or its workers, or someone the tenant did not let in (tenant). If the tenant, a family member who lives with them, or a guest caused it, the cause is not outside the people 83.51(4) names; say so. A roommate is not settled; give the open question on roommates. If they do not know the cause, say a work order, a technician's note, or the landlord's messages may show it.
4. The tenant did not give up ending the lease by paying rent while knowing of the problem: "the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Met when no rent was paid since they knew (tenant). If rent was paid, whether that gave up ending the lease over a problem still not fixed is not settled; give the open question on rent paid.

Steps, in order:

1. Deliver a written notice to the landlord in a way 83.56(4) allows: "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)). Handed over, regular mail, or certified mail fits. E-mail counts only as 83.505 allows: ask whether the tenant and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and read the lease's notices clause. A resident portal message or a text is not one of the ways the sentence names. For any other way, ask how the message reached the landlord and set it beside those ways.
2. The notice names the problem and says the tenant intends to end the lease because of it: "specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). Set the words of the tenant's message beside these words and say what you see. If the tenant says the message says nothing about ending the lease, it does not state that intention.
3. Seven days pass after the notice is delivered without the landlord fixing the problem: "within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). The program computes the date.

Whether the landlord's failure is 'material' is not settled; give the open question on that word.

### Not pay rent because of the problem, and raise it as a defense

The statute: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). All three conditions need to be met. This defense rests on the duty in 83.51(1) alone: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). A lease provision by itself does not reach it.

1. The problem is a failure of a duty in 83.51(1). Any one of these ways: the problem is with the structure or the plumbing (the tenant's pick, as for ending the lease); running water or hot water (not settled; give the open question on subsection (1) or (2)); 'something else' (ask what it is with); or a code where the unit is requires the landlord to fix it (outside the tool; send the tenant to the code enforcement office, as for ending the lease).
2. The landlord's duty was not changed in writing: the same condition as for ending the lease.
3. The tenant's side did not cause the problem: the same condition as for ending the lease, including the roommate question.

Steps, in order:

1. Deliver the written notice to the landlord: "7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). If it was handed over or mailed (regular or certified), it was delivered. For e-mail, a resident portal, a text, or anything else, the statute names no way of delivering this notice; give the open question on delivery.
2. The notice names the problem and says the tenant intends not to pay rent because of it: "specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). Set the words of the tenant's message beside these words and say what you see.
3. Seven days pass after the notice is delivered. The program computes the date.

Two open questions apply: what 'material' means, and the court's rule once a case is filed. If the record shows an eviction case was filed, apply the registry requirement itself (see the open question on court procedure); the tool does not compute its date.

### Overrides and exclusions

- A lease can alter the landlord's duty in the one case in condition 2 above. The tool does not decide its effect.
- "Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(2)(c)). This is about the items in 83.51(2): extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage, heat, running water, and hot water.
- Paying rent while knowing of the problem: "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a))

## Deadlines

The program computes two deadlines. Both are the landlord's, and both count from the date the tenant's written message was delivered to the landlord, not the date it was sent, once the tenant has confirmed that date. How the message was delivered matters to both: the ways are in the first step of each option above.

- Seven days to fix the problem after a notice to end the lease. It counts only when the message says the tenant intends to end the lease because of the problem. The statute: "If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement." (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) The program prints the date with this condition: the message was delivered in a way 83.56(4) allows and says the tenant intends to end the lease because of the problem. The tool does not decide that. Do not say the message meets it.
- Seven days after a notice not to pay rent. It counts only when the message says the tenant intends not to pay rent because of the problem. The statute: "The defense of a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) may be raised by the tenant if 7 days have elapsed after the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord, specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof." (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)) What follows from it: "A material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1) by the landlord is a complete defense to an action for possession based upon nonpayment of rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). The program prints the date with this condition: the message was delivered to the landlord and says the tenant intends not to pay rent because of the problem. The tool does not decide that either.

The program computes and prints every date. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself, not even for 'what if it ran from another day'. Whether a deadline has passed comes only from the program's deadlines (get_deadlines). The program prints the counting convention with each date: calendar days, the delivery day not counted, no weekend or holiday adjustment. It is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against these statutory deadlines. If the tenant asks how the days are counted, say so.

## What the statute does not settle

For each question below, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading with what it would mean for them, and pick none. Where one step works under every reading, say so.

- Which code applies. 83.51(1)(a) points to "the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(a)). Those codes are not in the tool, so whether a condition violates a code cannot be applied here; say so. The list in 83.51(1)(b) applies "Where there are no applicable building, housing, or health codes" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(b)).
- What 'material' means. Both 7-day periods concern a landlord who "materially fails to comply" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) or a "material noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). The stored text does not define it. Set the tenant's description of the problem, how long it has lasted, and the landlord's response beside the word.
  - A failure is material when it is a failure of a duty 83.51(1) lists (the codes; roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, other structural parts; the plumbing), whatever its size.
  - Material turns on degree: how serious the condition is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living in the unit, so a failure of a listed duty can still be minor.
- Subsection (1) or (2). 83.51(1) covers the codes and the structure and plumbing. 83.51(2)(a) adds, for a unit other than a single-family home or duplex and "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(2)(a)), extermination, locks and keys, common areas, garbage removal, and heat, running water, and hot water. 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) speak only of 83.51(1), and 83.51(2)(c) says part II does not let the tenant raise a noncompliance with subsection (2) as a defense to an action for possession. Apply the lists to the problem. What stays open is an item subsection (2) names that a code, or the plumbing 83.51(1)(b) names, may also cover, such as running water and hot water.
  - It is a subsection (1) duty when a code covers it or it is part of the plumbing, and 83.51(3) says that when subsection (1)'s duty is the same or greater, "the landlord’s duty is determined by subsection (1)" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(3)).
  - It is a subsection (2) duty because subsection (2) names it, so 83.56(1) and 83.60(1)(b) do not reach it.
- Court procedure. Once an eviction case is filed, 83.60(2) requires a tenant who raises "any defense other than payment" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(2)) to pay the rent into the registry of the court, within "5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(2)). Apply the requirement itself when the record shows a case was filed. The tool counts calendar days only and does not compute that date.
- Rent paid with knowledge. 83.56(5)(a) says that if the tenant "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)), the tenant waives the right "to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Set the rent paid since the tenant knew of the problem beside it, and whether the problem goes on.
  - A problem the landlord still has not fixed is a continuing noncompliance, so paying rent while it goes on does not waive ending the lease over it.
  - The noncompliance is the landlord's failure to fix the problem the tenant already knew of; paying rent with that knowledge waives ending the lease over it, and only a new or different failure starts over.
- A roommate who caused it. 83.51(4) leaves the landlord not responsible for conditions caused by "the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant’s family, or other person on the premises with the tenant’s consent" (Fla. Stat. 83.51(4)). The stored text does not say whether a roommate is such a person, in particular one the landlord placed in the unit. Set who caused the problem, and how the roommate came to live there, beside it.
  - A roommate who lives in the unit the tenant shares is on the premises with the tenant's consent, so the landlord is not responsible to the tenant for a condition the roommate caused by a negligent or wrongful act.
  - A roommate the landlord placed, under a lease of the roommate's own, is on the premises by the landlord's leave, not the tenant's consent, so 83.51(4) does not reach what the roommate caused, and the landlord stays responsible to the tenant.
- How the rent notice is delivered. 83.60(1)(b) runs its 7 days from "the delivery of written notice by the tenant to the landlord" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)) and names who may receive it, but names no way of delivering it. 83.56(4)'s ways are for "the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3)" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)) of 83.56, and 83.505 lets a party e-mail "any notices required under this part" (Fla. Stat. 83.505) once both have signed its addendum. Set beside it how the tenant's message reached the landlord.
  - 83.60(1)(b) names no way, so a written notice that reaches the landlord, or a person it names, is delivered however it was sent, by e-mail or the resident portal included.
  - The ways part II gives for notices apply to this one too, so a notice by e-mail counts only under an 83.505 addendum, and a resident portal request or a text is not a delivered notice.

## Letters

Every letter needs: today's date, the condition and when it started, the repair requested, the response deadline the tenant chooses, and how the tenant will deliver it. The tenant sends the letter; you send nothing. Read the lease's notices clause with search_lease and tell the tenant where and how the lease says notices go to the landlord.

The postures, each with its own line:

- preserve: Describes the condition and asks for the repair. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.51(1) duty, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.56(1) sentence, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant this. The 7-day periods the program computes run from the delivery of a written notice. In 83.56(1) that is a notice "specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)), and in 83.60(1)(b) one "specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant not to pay rent by reason thereof" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). The letter states the tenant's request and any sentences quoted in it. It is such a notice only if it states one of those intentions. Offer to apply this to the letter before the tenant sends it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Treating any written complaint as the notice in 83.56(1) or 83.60(1)(b). Each must state an intention: to end the lease, or not to pay rent.
- Saying the tenant may withhold rent for an item only 83.51(2) lists. 83.60(1)(b) speaks of "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). For ending the lease, 83.56(1) also reaches "material provisions of the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)), so read the lease's repair clause.
- Counting the 7 days yourself, or from the date the notice was sent instead of delivered. Whether they have passed comes from get_deadlines.
- Skipping 83.56(5)(a): paying rent with knowledge of the problem, and the continuing-noncompliance exception.
- Applying 83.51 to a condition the tenant's side caused (83.51(4)).
- Explaining rent withholding without 83.60(2): once a case is filed, any defense other than payment requires paying the rent into the registry of the court.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.name: get_statute_section
tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. WHEN YOU MOVE OUT, YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT. THE LANDLORD MUST PROVIDE YOU WRITTEN NOTICE IN PERSON, BY MAIL, OR BY E-MAIL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 83.505 , FLORIDA STATUTES, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT, OF THE LANDLORD’S INTENT TO IMPOSE A CLAIM AGAINST THE DEPOSIT. IF YOU DO NOT REPLY TO THE LANDLORD STATING YOUR OBJECTION TO THE CLAIM WITHIN 15 DAYS AFTER RECEIPT OF THE LANDLORD’S WRITTEN NOTICE, THE LANDLORD WILL COLLECT THE CLAIM AND MUST MAIL YOU THE REMAINING DEPOSIT, IF ANY. IF THE LANDLORD FAILS TO TIMELY PROVIDE YOU NOTICE, THE LANDLORD MUST RETURN THE DEPOSIT BUT MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT AGAINST YOU FOR DAMAGES. IF YOU FAIL TO TIMELY OBJECT TO A CLAIM, THE LANDLORD MAY COLLECT FROM THE DEPOSIT, BUT YOU MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT CLAIMING A REFUND. YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT. GENERALLY, THE PARTY IN WHOSE FAVOR A JUDGMENT IS RENDERED WILL BE AWARDED COSTS AND ATTORNEY FEES PAYABLE BY THE LOSING PARTY. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (3) The landlord or the landlord’s agent may disburse advance rents from the deposit account to the landlord’s benefit when the advance rental period commences and without notice to the tenant. For all other deposits: (a) Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement, if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement. If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . It is sent to you as required by s. 83.49 (3), Florida Statutes. You are hereby notified that you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice or I will be authorized to deduct my claim from your security deposit. Your objection must be sent to (landlord’s address) . If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant. (b) Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages. The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action. (c) If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney. The court shall advance the cause on the calendar. (d) Compliance with this section by an individual or business entity authorized to conduct business in this state, including Florida-licensed real estate brokers and sales associates, constitutes compliance with all other relevant Florida Statutes pertaining to security deposits held pursuant to a rental agreement or other landlord-tenant relationship. Enforcement personnel shall look solely to this section to determine compliance. This section prevails over any conflicting provisions in chapter 475 and in other sections of the Florida Statutes, and shall operate to permit licensed real estate brokers to disburse security deposits and deposit money without having to comply with the notice and settlement procedures contained in s. 475.25 (1)(d). (4) This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs including s. 202, s. 221(d)(3) and (4), s. 236, or s. 8 of the National Housing Act, as amended, other than for rent stabilization. With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes. (5) Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year, must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached. Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it. (6) For the purposes of this part, a renewal of an existing rental agreement shall be considered a new rental agreement, and any security deposit carried forward shall be considered a new security deposit. (7) Upon the sale or transfer of title of the rental property from one owner to another, or upon a change in the designated rental agent, any and all security deposits or advance rents being held for the benefit of the tenants shall be transferred to the new owner or agent, together with any earned interest and with an accurate accounting showing the amounts to be credited to each tenant account. Upon the transfer of such funds and records to the new owner or agent, and upon transmittal of a written receipt therefor, the transferor is free from the obligation imposed in subsection (1) to hold such moneys on behalf of the tenant. There is a rebuttable presumption that any new owner or agent received the security deposit from the previous owner or agent; however, this presumption is limited to 1 month’s rent. This subsection does not excuse the landlord or agent for a violation of other provisions of this section while in possession of such deposits. (8) Any person licensed under s. 509.241 , unless excluded by the provisions of this part, who fails to comply with this part is subject to a fine or to the suspension or revocation of his or her license by the Division of Hotels and Restaurants of the Department of Business and Professional Regulation in the manner provided in s. 509.261 . (9) In those cases in which interest is required to be paid to the tenant, the landlord must pay directly to the tenant, or credit against the current month’s rent, the interest due to the tenant at least once annually. However, a landlord is not required to pay interest to a tenant who wrongfully terminates his or her tenancy before the end of the rental term. tool_calls.result: 83.56 Termination of rental agreement. — (1) If the landlord materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement. If the failure to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement is due to causes beyond the control of the landlord and the landlord has made and continues to make every reasonable effort to correct the failure to comply, the rental agreement may be terminated or altered by the parties, as follows: (a) If the landlord’s failure to comply renders the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant vacates, the tenant shall not be liable for rent during the period the dwelling unit remains uninhabitable. (b) If the landlord’s failure to comply does not render the dwelling unit untenantable and the tenant remains in occupancy, the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance. (2) If the tenant materially fails to comply with s. 83.52 or material provisions of the rental agreement, other than a failure to pay rent, or reasonable rules or regulations, the landlord may: (a) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure it or if the noncompliance constitutes a subsequent or continuing noncompliance within 12 months of a written warning by the landlord of a similar violation, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance and the landlord’s intent to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of noncompliance which are of a nature that the tenant should not be given an opportunity to cure include, but are not limited to, destruction, damage, or misuse of the landlord’s or other tenants’ property by intentional act; an act of fraudulent entry of a residential dwelling unit which violates s. 817.537 (2), regardless of whether criminal proceedings have commenced; or a subsequent or continued unreasonable disturbance. In such event, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement, and the tenant shall have 7 days from the date that the notice is delivered to vacate the premises. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are advised that your lease is terminated effective immediately. You shall have 7 days from the delivery of this letter to vacate the premises. This action is taken because (cite the noncompliance) . (b) If such noncompliance is of a nature that the tenant should be given an opportunity to cure it, deliver a written notice to the tenant specifying the noncompliance, including a notice that, if the noncompliance is not corrected within 7 days from the date that the written notice is delivered, the landlord shall terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof. Examples of such noncompliance include, but are not limited to, activities in contravention of the lease or this part such as having or permitting unauthorized pets, guests, or vehicles; parking in an unauthorized manner or permitting such parking; or failing to keep the premises clean and sanitary. If such noncompliance recurs within 12 months after notice, an eviction action may commence without delivering a subsequent notice pursuant to paragraph (a) or this paragraph. The notice shall be in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that (cite the noncompliance) . Demand is hereby made that you remedy the noncompliance within 7 days of receipt of this notice or your lease shall be deemed terminated and you shall vacate the premises upon such termination. If this same conduct or conduct of a similar nature is repeated within 12 months, your tenancy is subject to termination without further warning and without your being given an opportunity to cure the noncompliance. (3) If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement. Legal holidays for the purpose of this section shall be court-observed holidays only. The 3-day notice shall contain a statement in substantially the following form: You are hereby notified that you are indebted to me in the sum of dollars for the rent and use of the premises (address of leased premises, including county) , Florida, now occupied by you and that I demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays) from the date of delivery of this notice, to wit: on or before the day of , (year) . (landlord’s name, address and phone number) (4) The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence. The notice requirements of subsections (1)-(3) may not be waived in the rental agreement. (5)(a) If the landlord accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant or accepts performance by the tenant of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, or if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord or accepts performance by the landlord of any other provision of the rental agreement that is at variance with its provisions, the landlord or tenant waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance. However, a landlord does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period. If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must: 1. Provide the tenant with a receipt stating the date and amount received and the agreed-upon date and balance of rent due before filing an action for possession; 2. Place the amount of partial rent accepted from the tenant in the registry of the court upon filing the action for possession; or 3. Post a new 3-day notice reflecting the new amount due. (b) Any tenant who wishes to defend against an action by the landlord for possession of the unit for noncompliance of the rental agreement or of relevant statutes must comply with s. 83.60 (2). The court may not set a date for mediation or trial unless the provisions of s. 83.60 (2) have been met, but must enter a default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue immediately if the tenant fails to comply with s. 83.60 (2). (c) This subsection does not apply to that portion of rent subsidies received from a local, state, or national government or an agency of local, state, or national government; however, waiver will occur if an action has not been instituted within 45 days after the landlord obtains actual knowledge of the noncompliance. (6) If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 23, ch. 82-66; s. 6, ch. 83-151; s. 14, ch. 83-217; s. 6, ch. 87-195; s. 6, ch. 93-255; s. 6, ch. 94-170; s. 1373, ch. 95-147; s. 5, ch. 99-6; s. 8, ch. 2013-136; s. 5, ch. 2025-16; s. 2, ch. 2026-143.

tool_calls.result: 83.51 Landlord’s obligation to maintain premises. — (1) The landlord at all times during the tenancy shall: (a) Comply with the requirements of applicable building, housing, and health codes; or (b) Where there are no applicable building, housing, or health codes, maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair and capable of resisting normal forces and loads and the plumbing in reasonable working condition. The landlord, at commencement of the tenancy, must ensure that screens are installed in a reasonable condition. Thereafter, the landlord must repair damage to screens once annually, when necessary, until termination of the rental agreement. The landlord is not required to maintain a mobile home or other structure owned by the tenant. The landlord’s obligations under this subsection may be altered or modified in writing with respect to a single-family home or duplex. (2)(a) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, in addition to the requirements of subsection (1), the landlord of a dwelling unit other than a single-family home or duplex shall, at all times during the tenancy, make reasonable provisions for: 1. The extermination of rats, mice, roaches, ants, wood-destroying organisms, and bedbugs. If the tenant must vacate the premises for such extermination, the landlord is not liable for damages but must abate the rent. The landlord must provide 7 days’ written notice, in person, by mail, or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 , to the tenant if the tenant must temporarily vacate the premises for extermination pursuant to this subparagraph. A tenant is only required to vacate the premises for a period of time not to exceed 4 days. 2. Locks and keys. 3. The clean and safe condition of common areas. 4. Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor. 5. Functioning facilities for heat during winter, running water, and hot water. (b) Unless otherwise agreed in writing, at the commencement of the tenancy of a single-family home or duplex, the landlord shall install working smoke detection devices. As used in this paragraph, the term “smoke detection device” means an electrical or battery-operated device which detects visible or invisible particles of combustion and which is listed by Underwriters Laboratories, Inc., Factory Mutual Laboratories, Inc., or any other nationally recognized testing laboratory using nationally accepted testing standards. (c) Nothing in this part authorizes the tenant to raise a noncompliance by the landlord with this subsection as a defense to an action for possession under s. 83.59 . (d) This subsection shall not apply to a mobile home owned by a tenant. (e) Nothing contained in this subsection prohibits the landlord from providing in the rental agreement that the tenant is obligated to pay costs or charges for garbage removal, water, fuel, or utilities. (3) If the duty imposed by subsection (1) is the same or greater than any duty imposed by subsection (2), the landlord’s duty is determined by subsection (1). (4) The landlord is not responsible to the tenant under this section for conditions created or caused by the negligent or wrongful act or omission of the tenant, a member of the tenant’s family, or other person on the premises with the tenant’s consent. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 22, ch. 82-66; s. 4, ch. 87-195; s. 1, ch. 90-133; s. 3, ch. 93-255; s. 444, ch. 95-147; s. 8, ch. 97-95; s. 6, ch. 2013-136; s. 4, ch. 2025-16.
